lessons.title: CRR and SLR: How the RBI Controls Bank Lending Capacity

body.text: The repo rate sets the price of money. CRR and SLR set how much of every deposit a bank is allowed to lend at all. Change the price and credit gets cheaper or dearer; change the quantity and banks physically have more or less money to push into the economy.

children.text: In the last lesson you saw how the corridor of policy rates steers the cost of overnight money. This lesson covers the RBI's other lever: rules that lock away a slice of every rupee deposited in a bank. They are less talked about than the repo rate, but when the RBI changes them, lakhs of crores move through the banking system in a matter of weeks.
Start With NDTL: The Base Everything Is Measured On

markDefs.definition: A bank's deposits and similar obligations to the public, such as savings, current and fixed deposits, net of certain interbank balances. CRR and SLR are calculated as a percentage of this figure.

children.text: Both ratios are calculated as a percentage of a bank's
net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)
. In plain terms, NDTL is mostly the deposits you and millions of others have placed with the bank: savings accounts, current accounts and fixed deposits.
Demand liabilities
are deposits you can withdraw any time: savings and current accounts.
Time liabilities
are deposits locked for a period: fixed and recurring deposits.
Net
means certain interbank amounts are netted off, so the same money is not counted twice across banks.
CRR: Cash Locked Away at the RBI

markDefs.definition: The percentage of a bank's NDTL that it must keep as cash balances with the RBI. These balances earn no interest and cannot be lent out.

children.text: The
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
is the share of NDTL that a bank must keep as a cash balance in its account with the RBI. That money cannot be lent, cannot be invested, and earns nothing.

stats.label: CRR
stats.context: Of NDTL, held as cash with the RBI

stats.label: Daily minimum
stats.context: Of required CRR on every day of the fortnight

stats.label: SLR
stats.context: Of NDTL, held by the bank in safe assets

children.text: Banks do not have to hit the exact CRR figure every day. The requirement is measured as an average over a two-week reporting fortnight, with a floor of 90% of the required amount on any single day. That flexibility lets banks absorb daily swings in deposits without breaching the rule.
Why Lock Money Away at All?
Safety buffer:
a slice of every deposit is always held in the safest possible form, with the central bank itself.
Liquidity control:
raising CRR drains cash from the banking system instantly; cutting it releases cash. This is the RBI's bluntest and fastest liquidity tool.
Signal:
a CRR change tells markets whether the RBI wants more or less money flowing through banks, independently of the repo rate.
SLR: Safe Assets the Bank Holds Itself

markDefs.definition: The percentage of NDTL a bank must hold in specified liquid assets such as cash, gold and unencumbered government securities. Unlike CRR, these assets stay with the bank and can earn interest.

children.text: The
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
requires banks to hold 18% of NDTL in liquid, safe assets. Unlike CRR, this money stays on the bank's own books and usually earns a return, because most of it is invested in government securities.
Assets that count towards SLR include cash, gold, and government securities that are unencumbered, meaning they are not already pledged as collateral for a loan.

body.title: Complete the Rule
body.textWithBlank: To meet SLR, banks mostly hold cash, gold and unencumbered ___ securities.
body.explanation: Government securities, often called G-Secs. They are the bulk of every bank's SLR holdings because they are safe, liquid and pay interest, unlike cash or gold.

body.title: Quick Check: Which One Costs More?
body.question: Per rupee locked away, which requirement is more expensive for a bank, and why?
options: SLR, because it is a higher percentage of NDTL
CRR, because the cash held with the RBI earns no interest
Both cost the same, because neither can be lent to customers
SLR, because government securities can lose value
body.explanation: SLR is a bigger share of deposits, but those government securities pay interest. CRR balances earn nothing at all, so every rupee of CRR is a rupee of pure lost income. That is why banks lobby hardest for CRR cuts, and why a CRR cut directly improves bank profitability.

children.text: Follow ₹1,00,000 Crore of Deposits
Take a hypothetical bank, call it Bank Alpha, with NDTL of ₹1,00,000 crore. Here is how the rules split that money today.

body.title: Where Bank Alpha's ₹1,00,000 Crore of NDTL Goes (₹ crore)

data.label: SLR: safe assets held by the bank
Available for loans and other investments

body.latex: \text{Annual cost of CRR} = \text{CRR balance} \times \text{Return the bank could have earned}
body.caption: The cost is the income forgone on money that must sit idle

children.text: If Bank Alpha could have lent that ₹3,000 crore at 8%, the CRR costs it about ₹240 crore of income every year. That is why the size of CRR matters so much to bank shareholders.

body.title: What Does a CRR Cut Put in Bank Alpha's Pocket?
body.prompt: The RBI cuts CRR by 100 basis points, from 4% to 3%. Bank Alpha has NDTL of ₹1,00,000 crore and lends all the freed cash at 8% a year. How much extra annual interest income does it earn, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: A 1 percentage point cut frees 1% of NDTL: ₹1,00,000 crore × 1% = ₹1,000 crore. Lent at 8%, that earns ₹1,000 crore × 8% = ₹80 crore a year. In reality, banks earn less than this, because part of the freed cash sits in lower-yielding assets and deposit rates also adjust, but the direction is clear: CRR cuts support bank margins.

children.text: CRR in Action: Six Years of Big Moves
Unlike SLR, CRR has been actively used in recent years. Each move tells you what the RBI was trying to do with liquidity at the time.

body.title: Cash Reserve Ratio at Key Dates (%)
What Each CRR Move Was For

events.title: Cut from 4% to 3%
events.description: Part of the RBI's COVID emergency package, releasing about ₹1.37 lakh crore to keep banks liquid as the economy shut down.

events.title: Restored to 4% in two steps
events.description: As the emergency faded, the RBI gradually took back the extra liquidity.

events.title: Hiked to 4.5%
events.description: Announced alongside the off-cycle repo hike as inflation surged after the Russia-Ukraine war. It drained cash to reinforce the tightening.

events.title: Temporary 10% incremental CRR
events.description: Banks had to hold 10% of the increase in NDTL between 19 May and 28 July 2023 as extra CRR, soaking up about ₹1 lakh crore that flooded in after ₹2,000 notes were withdrawn. It was fully released in phases by 7 October 2023.

events.title: Cut to 4%
events.description: Two 25 basis point tranches released about ₹1.16 lakh crore as liquidity tightened.

events.title: Cut to 3% in four steps
events.description: Delivered in 25 basis point tranches in fortnights starting 6 September, 4 October, 1 November and 29 November 2025, releasing about ₹2.5 lakh crore to support lending and help rate cuts reach borrowers.

body.title: Work Out the Size of the Banking System
body.prompt: The RBI said a 100 basis point CRR cut would release about ₹2.5 lakh crore. Since CRR is a percentage of NDTL, roughly how large is the total NDTL of the banking system, in ₹ lakh crore?
body.explanation: A 100 basis point cut releases 1% of NDTL. If 1% of NDTL = ₹2.5 lakh crore, then NDTL ≈ ₹2.5 lakh crore ÷ 0.01 = ₹250 lakh crore. This quick reverse calculation is useful: every 25 basis point CRR move releases or absorbs roughly ₹62,500 crore of bank cash at that system size.

body.text: Notice the incremental CRR of 2023. It did not change the headline CRR at all. It applied only to new deposits over a specific window. That made it a precise, temporary tool for a one-off liquidity surge, and it is exactly the tool markets began discussing again in August 2026, when banking system liquidity swelled far into surplus.

children.text: SLR: From 38.5% to 18%

markDefs.definition: Policies that force savers' money into government debt or hold interest rates artificially low, often to make government borrowing cheaper, at the cost of private lending and returns.

children.text: In 1990, Indian banks had to hold 38.5% of NDTL under SLR and another 15% under CRR. More than half of every deposit was locked into cash or government bonds before a single rupee could be lent to a business. This was a form of
financial repression
: a guaranteed, captive buyer for government debt.

The Narasimham Committee of 1991 recommended bringing SLR down to 25% and CRR towards 3% to 5%, to free bank money for productive lending. SLR reached 25% within a few years of the reforms and was cut in steps over two decades to 18%, where it has stayed since April 2020.

body.title: Share of Deposits Locked Away: 1990 vs Today (%)

body.text: The 18% SLR is a minimum, not what banks actually hold. Most banks keep government securities well above 18% of NDTL, because those bonds also count towards the Liquidity Coverage Ratio under Basel III rules and are needed as collateral to borrow from the RBI through repo. So a small SLR cut today would free less lending capacity than the headline number suggests.

body.title: Go Deeper: The Money Multiplier and Why It Is Only a Rough Guide

children.text: Textbooks often say that a reserve requirement creates a money multiplier. If banks must hold a fraction of every deposit in reserve and lend out the rest, each loan gets redeposited somewhere, and part of that is lent again.

content.caption: At a 3% CRR alone, the theoretical multiplier would be 1 ÷ 0.03 ≈ 33

children.text: In reality, India's multiplier is far smaller. People hold part of their money as cash rather than redepositing it, banks hold SLR assets and extra liquidity on top of CRR, and lending depends on whether creditworthy borrowers actually want loans. Modern central banks, including the RBI, treat the multiplier as a useful intuition, not a precise formula. What matters in practice is that lower reserve requirements give banks more room to lend if demand exists.
Price vs Quantity: When the RBI Reaches for CRR

body.title: Repo Rate vs CRR as Policy Tools

columns.label: Repo rate
points: Changes the price of money for everyone
Set by the MPC by vote
Transmission to loan rates takes weeks to months
The main signal of policy direction

columns.label: CRR
points: Changes the quantity of cash banks can deploy
Decided by the RBI as a liquidity measure
Moves lakhs of crores into or out of banks within a fortnight
Directly changes banks' cost of funds and margins

children.text: The two often work together. In June 2025, the RBI cut the repo rate by 50 basis points and announced the 100 basis point CRR cut on the same day. The rate cut lowered the price of money; the CRR cut made sure banks had enough cheap cash to actually pass that lower price on to borrowers.

body.title: What If the RBI Imposes an Incremental CRR?
body.scenario: It is September 2026. Banking system liquidity is in a large surplus, the call rate is trading below the 5.25% repo rate, and the RBI expects CPI inflation to peak at 5.9% in October to December. Bond market participants are discussing whether the RBI will impose an incremental CRR on new deposits before considering any repo rate hike.
body.prompt: If the RBI does impose an incremental CRR, what would you expect to happen to (a) the call rate, (b) bank stocks on the NSE, and (c) FD rates? Explain your reasoning.
body.modelAnswer: (a) The call rate should rise towards the 5.25% repo rate. An incremental CRR impounds a slice of new deposits as idle cash with the RBI, which reduces the surplus cash banks have to lend overnight, so the overnight rate moves up towards the policy rate. That is the point of the measure: tighten liquidity so the existing repo rate actually bites. (b) Bank stocks, and the Nifty Bank index, would likely react negatively in the short run, because more money earns zero interest, which squeezes net interest margins. The effect should be modest if the measure is temporary and targeted, as in 2023. (c) FD rates could edge up over time. With less surplus cash, banks compete a little harder for deposits. It is also a signal that the RBI is leaning towards tighter conditions, which markets would read as reducing the chance of further rate cuts.

An extra CRR applied only to growth in deposits over a set period, used as a temporary tool to absorb surplus liquidity.
The two-week period over which CRR compliance is averaged, with at least 90% required on each day.
Securities not already pledged as collateral, and therefore eligible to count towards SLR.
Forcing savings into government debt through high reserve rules or capped rates.

body.label: Screener.in: Compare Bank Margins
body.description: Search any listed bank, such as SBI or HDFC Bank, and track its net interest income and margins across quarters around the September to November 2025 CRR cuts.

body.title: See the CRR Cut in Real Data
steps: On Screener.in, open a large bank like SBI and note its net interest margin for the quarter ended June 2025
Compare it with the quarters ended December 2025 and March 2026, after all four CRR tranches took effect
Check whether margins held up even as repo rate cuts lowered loan yields
Read one bank's investor presentation and look for any mention of the CRR cut
Note the current CRR and SLR on the RBI homepage and check whether anything has changed since this lesson

points: CRR and SLR are calculated on NDTL, which is mostly a bank's deposits.
CRR is 3% of NDTL held as cash with the RBI and earns no interest, so it is a direct cost to banks.
SLR is 18% of NDTL held by banks in cash, gold or government securities, which do earn interest.
CRR is the RBI's fastest liquidity lever: the 2025 cut from 4% to 3% released about ₹2.5 lakh crore in four tranches.
An incremental CRR, like the 10% measure of 2023, targets only new deposits and is used to absorb temporary liquidity surges.
SLR has fallen from 38.5% in 1990 to 18% today, freeing bank money for lending, but banks still hold well above the minimum.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Bank Alpha is a hypothetical example. CRR and SLR levels are as of the RBI's August 2026 policy and can change.
